News Topic Classification for Kinyarwanda and Kirundi (KINNEWS & KIRNEWS)¶

Goal: read a news article written in Kinyarwanda or Kirundi and predict its topic (politics, sport, economy, health, ...), then offer this as a web app: a FastAPI server that answers requests and serves an HTML page where the user types the text. Data: KINNEWS and KIRNEWS (Niyongabo et al., COLING 2020): news articles collected from Rwandan and Burundian news websites and newspapers.

Assignment checklist: where is everything?¶

Assignment requirement Where in this project
A meaningful classification problem in an African language News topic classification in Kinyarwanda (DATASET = "kinnews") or Kirundi (DATASET = "kirnews")
A labelled dataset, and how it was obtained Section 2: the zip files of the dataset are downloaded from GitHub (the source used by the Hugging Face dataset); the articles come from news websites and newspapers
How the categories were defined Table "The topics" below
How the text was preprocessed Section 4: one function, basic_cleaning(), plus removal of empty, duplicate and conflicting articles
How the data was split into train / validation / test Section 5: general stratified 70 / 15 / 15 split
A baseline Experiment 0 (majority class) and Experiment 1 (TF-IDF + Logistic Regression)
Machine-learning approaches from the course Word2Vec (Exp. 5) · CNN (Exp. 3) · LSTM / BiLSTM + attention (Exp. 4, 5) · Transformer (Exp. 6)
Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 Every experiment prints them; Section 8 compares all models
Error analysis Section 9
Web interface where a user types text and gets the category Section 10 saves the model into the models/ folder; FastAPI (api/main.py) loads it and serves the HTML page (frontend/index.html)

The topics (how the categories are defined)¶

Each article has one topic label, given with the dataset. The 14 possible topics are numbered 1 to 14 in the data files.

# Topic # Topic
1 politics 8 tourism
2 sport 9 culture
3 economy 10 fashion
4 health 11 religion
5 entertainment 12 environment
6 history 13 education
7 technology 14 relationship
  • Kinyarwanda (KINNEWS) uses all 14 topics. Kirundi (KIRNEWS) uses 12 (no tourism and no fashion).
  • Topics with too few articles to learn and test fairly are removed and listed (setting MIN_ARTICLES_PER_CLASS).

⚠️ A data-quality finding you must mention in your report: the original files contain a very large share of duplicate articles (about half of KINNEWS and more than half of KIRNEWS), and many test articles also appear in the training set. If we did not remove them, the scores would be too high, because the model would be tested on articles it has already seen. Section 3 measures this and Section 4 removes it.

The experiments: 1 model each¶

Every experiment is one model with one settings dictionary. You run it with one line and get 4 things back:

model, val_probs, val_scores, cv_scores = run_experiment("name", "short notes")
# Experiment Key idea
0 Baseline: majority class always predicts the most common topic (the score every model must beat)
1 Logistic Regression word + 2-word phrases (TF-IDF), class weights
2 Naive Bayes Complement NB (made for imbalanced classes)
3 CNN finds key phrases in the article
4 BiLSTM + attention reads the article in both directions and focuses on important words
5 BiLSTM + Word2Vec the same BiLSTM, but starting from Word2Vec word embeddings trained on our articles
6 Transformer (AfroXLMR) a large pretrained multilingual model that knows Kinyarwanda and Kirundi, fine-tuned (needs a GPU; skipped automatically without one)
7 (bonus) Ensemble average of the models above

All experiments use the same cleaned data and the same split. Then we compare all models on validation, pick the best, and score the test set once.

Words you will see¶

Word Meaning
macro-F1 Average F1 over all topics, so small topics count as much as big ones. Our main score.
precision / recall / F1 Precision: of the articles we put in a topic, how many were right. Recall: of the real articles of a topic, how many we found. F1 combines both.
class weights Mistakes on rarer topics cost more during training.
TF-IDF Turns text into numbers; words that are special to an article get a high weight.
Word2Vec Learns a vector for every word so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors.
cross-validation (CV) Train/test 5 times on different slices of the training data to check the score is stable.
validation set Used to choose settings. Test set is only used once at the end.

    here = Path.cwd().resolve()
    for folder in [here, *here.parents]:
        if (folder / "data").is_dir() and ((folder / "notebook").is_dir() or (folder / "notebooks").is_dir()
                                           or (folder / ".git").exists() or (folder / "api").is_dir()):
            return folder
    return here.parent if here.name in {"notebook", "notebooks"} else here

4. Clean the data¶

We clean the articles with one function, basic_cleaning(), in the same way for every experiment (and later in the app).

What we clean (and why)¶

Step Why
Decode HTML codes (&amp; → &) web-page noise
Normalise unicode (NFKC) turns special spaces (\xa0) and look-alike characters into one form
Remove invisible characters they split words in two
Remove links and e-mail addresses random strings, no topic information
Lower-case Inkino and inkino become one word
Squeeze spaces tidy text

What we deliberately do not do¶

  • No stop-word removal, no stemming: reliable tools for Kinyarwanda and Kirundi are not available, and a wrong rule would damage the text.
  • Numbers and punctuation stay: scores, dates and amounts are useful hints (sport, economy).

After that we remove empty articles, articles with conflicting labels (the same text labelled with two different topics) and duplicates (same text; the first copy is kept). Because the train file comes first, a test article that is also in train is removed from test.

In [7]:
# ── ONE function does all the cleaning: one clear step per line ───────────
def basic_cleaning(text):
    text = html.unescape(str(text))                                    # &amp; -> &
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)                         # \xa0 and look-alike characters -> one form
    text = re.sub(r"[\u200b\u2060\ufeff\u00ad]", "", text)             # invisible characters
    text = re.sub(r"https?://\S+|www\.\S+", " ", text)                 # links
    text = re.sub(r"\S+@\S+\.\S+", " ", text)                          # e-mail addresses
    text = text.lower()                                                # lower-case
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()                           # extra spaces

# Quick test on a made-up example
example = "Primus Ligue\xa0: Imirwi &amp; amakipe  https://example.com/x"
print("before:", repr(example))
print("after :", repr(basic_cleaning(example)))

5. Split the data¶

  • SPLIT_MODE = "general" (default): all cleaned, unique articles are split once into 70% train / 15% validation / 15% test, stratified by topic (every split has the same topic proportions), with a fixed seed. Every experiment uses exactly these same three sets, so the comparison is fair.
  • SPLIT_MODE = "official": keep the official train and test files (after removing duplicates). The validation set is 15% of the train file.
In [10]:
if SPLIT_MODE == "general":
    # Step 1: 70% train, 30% "rest".   Step 2: split "rest" half/half into validation and test.

    validation, test = train_test_split(rest, test_size=TEST_SHARE / (VAL_SHARE + TEST_SHARE),
                                        stratify=rest["category"], random_state=SEED)

6. Helper functions (used by every experiment)¶

Small helpers so that every model is scored in exactly the same way:

  • get_scores(y_true, probs) → macro-F1, weighted-F1, accuracy, log loss
  • show_report(...) → per-topic precision / recall / F1 and a confusion matrix
  • register_model(...) → keeps every trained model in one place (used by the comparison, the error analysis and the app)

All models give probabilities (one per topic) and the predicted topic is the one with the highest probability.

In [11]:
ALL_CLASSES = list(range(N_CLASSES))

def get_scores(y_true, probs):
    """Compute the 4 scores from predicted probabilities."""
    probs = np.clip(probs, 1e-12, 1.0)
    probs = probs / probs.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    pred = probs.argmax(axis=1)
    return {"macro_f1": f1_score(y_true, pred, average="macro", labels=ALL_CLASSES, zero_division=0),
            "weighted_f1": f1_score(y_true, pred, average="weighted", labels=ALL_CLASSES, zero_division=0),
            "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, pred),
            "log_loss": log_loss(y_true, probs, labels=ALL_CLASSES)}

def plot_confusion(title, y_true, pred):
    """Confusion matrix as percentages of each TRUE topic (rows add up to 100%)."""
    counts = confusion_matrix(y_true, pred, labels=ALL_CLASSES)
    share = counts / np.maximum(counts.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True), 1)
    size = max(5, 0.55 * N_CLASSES + 2)
    plt.figure(figsize=(size, size * 0.85))
    sns.heatmap(share, annot=True, fmt=".0%", cmap="Blues", xticklabels=LABELS, yticklabels=LABELS,
                cbar=False, annot_kws={"size": 7}, vmin=0, vmax=1)
    plt.title(title); plt.xlabel("predicted topic"); plt.ylabel("true topic")
    plt.xticks(rotation=60, ha="right"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

def show_report(title, y_true, probs):
    """Per-topic precision / recall / F1 and a confusion matrix."""
    pred = probs.argmax(axis=1)
    print(classification_report(y_true, pred, labels=ALL_CLASSES, target_names=LABELS, zero_division=0, digits=3))
    plot_confusion(title, y_true, pred)

experiment_log = []      # one row per experiment, so we can compare everything at the end

def log_experiment(name, notes, settings, val_scores, cv_scores):
    experiment_log.append({"experiment": name, "notes": notes, "settings": str(settings),
                           "val_macro_f1": val_scores["macro_f1"], "val_accuracy": val_scores["accuracy"],
                           "val_log_loss": val_scores["log_loss"],
                           "cv_macro_f1": None if cv_scores is None else cv_scores["macro_f1_mean"]})

# Every trained model is stored here, so the final comparison, the error analysis and the app can use them all
MODELS = {}        # key -> model object (every model has .predict_proba(list_of_texts))
RESULT_INFO = {}   # key -> experiment name, validation scores, cv scores, settings

def register_model(key, experiment, model, val_scores, cv_scores, settings=None):
    MODELS[key] = model
    RESULT_INFO[key] = {"experiment": experiment, "val_scores": val_scores, "cv_scores": cv_scores,
                        "settings": dict(settings or {})}

Experiment 0: Baseline (majority class)¶

Idea: the simplest "model": it ignores the text and always predicts the topic shares of the training data (so it always answers with the most common topic). Every real model must beat this. If a model scores about the same, it has learned nothing.

In [12]:
settings = {"strategy": "prior"}      # "prior" = always predict the topic shares of the training data

def run_experiment(name, notes):
    """Train the baseline with `settings`, then score it on validation and with 5-fold CV."""
    model = DummyClassifier(strategy=settings["strategy"])

    cv = cross_validate(model, train_text, y_train, cv=5, scoring="f1_macro")
    cv_scores = {"macro_f1_mean": cv["test_score"].mean(), "macro_f1_std": cv["test_score"].std()}

    model.fit(train_text, y_train)
    val_probs = model.predict_proba(val_text)
    val_scores = get_scores(y_val, val_probs)

    log_experiment(name, notes, settings, val_scores, cv_scores)
    return model, val_probs, val_scores, cv_scores

Experiment 1: TF-IDF + Logistic Regression¶

Idea: turn each article into numbers with TF-IDF (single words and 2-word phrases) and learn which words point to which topic. A strong, fast text baseline. Class weights = "balanced": mistakes on the rarer topics count more, which helps small topics like education or fashion.

In [13]:
settings = {"ngram_range": (1, 2), "class_weight": "balanced", "C": 10.0, "max_features": 300000}

def run_experiment(name, notes):
    """Train Logistic Regression with `settings`, then score it on validation and with 5-fold CV."""
    # 1. Build the model: TF-IDF features -> Logistic Regression
    model = make_pipeline(
        TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=settings["ngram_range"], sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2, max_features=settings["max_features"]),
        LogisticRegression(C=settings["C"], class_weight=settings["class_weight"], max_iter=300))

    # 2. Cross-validation on the TRAINING data (checks the score is stable)
    cv = cross_validate(model, train_text, y_train, cv=5, scoring="f1_macro", n_jobs=-1)
    cv_scores = {"macro_f1_mean": cv["test_score"].mean(), "macro_f1_std": cv["test_score"].std()}

    # 3. Train on the full training set and score on the VALIDATION set
    model.fit(train_text, y_train)
    val_probs = model.predict_proba(val_text)
    val_scores = get_scores(y_val, val_probs)

    log_experiment(name, notes, settings, val_scores, cv_scores)
    return model, val_probs, val_scores, cv_scores

Experiment 2: TF-IDF + Complement Naive Bayes¶

Idea: count how often each word appears in each topic and use Bayes' rule. It is the fastest model here. Complement NB is a version designed for imbalanced classes. alpha is the smoothing strength (how much probability unseen words get).

Tools for the neural experiments (CNN, BiLSTM, Word2Vec)¶

A neural network cannot read text, so we convert it step by step:

article  ->  words  ->  numbers (vocabulary)  ->  same length (pad/cut)  ->  network  ->  one probability per topic

This section prepares everything once:

  1. tokenize: split an article into words.
  2. vocab: a dictionary word → number, built from training articles only.
  3. NeuralTextClassifier: a small wrapper so a neural model has the same .predict_proba(texts) as the scikit-learn models.
  4. train_network: the training loop. After each epoch it checks validation macro-F1 and keeps the best epoch (early stopping).
In [17]:
PAD, UNK = 0, 1       # 0 = padding, 1 = unknown word

def tokenize(text):
    """Split into words (letters, digits and apostrophes)."""
    return re.findall(r"[\w']+", str(text).lower())

# Build the vocabulary from TRAINING articles only (words seen at least twice)
word_counts = Counter(word for text in train_text for word in tokenize(text))
vocab = {"<pad>": PAD, "<unk>": UNK}
for word, count in sorted(word_counts.items()):
    if count >= 2:
        vocab[word] = len(vocab)
print("Vocabulary size:", len(vocab))

def encode(texts, max_len):
    """Texts -> tensor of word numbers, all exactly max_len long."""
    rows = []
    for text in texts:
        ids = [vocab.get(word, UNK) for word in tokenize(text)[:max_len]]   # cut long articles
        rows.append(ids + [PAD] * (max_len - len(ids)))                     # pad short articles
    return torch.tensor(rows, dtype=torch.long)

class NeuralTextClassifier:
    """Wraps a trained network so it can be used like a scikit-learn model: model.predict_proba(texts)."""
    def __init__(self, network, max_len):
        self.network, self.max_len = network, max_len

    @torch.no_grad()
    def predict_proba(self, texts):
        self.network.eval()
        x = encode(texts, self.max_len)
        out = []
        for i in range(0, len(x), 256):                          # small batches to save memory
            logits = self.network(x[i:i + 256].to(device))
            out.append(F.softmax(logits, dim=1).cpu().numpy())
        return np.vstack(out)

Vocabulary size: 15156
In [18]:
def train_network(network, settings):
    """Train a network with Adam. Stops early when validation macro-F1 stops improving.
    Returns the best version of the network."""
    set_seed(SEED)
    network = network.to(device)
    x_train = encode(train_text, settings["max_len"])

    # Class weights: rare topics get a bigger penalty when they are misclassified
    weights = None
    if settings["class_weights"]:
        w = compute_class_weight("balanced", classes=np.arange(N_CLASSES), y=y_train)
        weights = torch.tensor(w, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
    loss_function = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=weights)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(network.parameters(), lr=settings["lr"])
    loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(x_train, torch.tensor(y_train)), batch_size=settings["batch_size"],
                        shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED))

    best_f1, best_weights, epochs_without_gain, history = -1.0, None, 0, []
    for epoch in range(1, settings["epochs"] + 1):
        # ---- train for one epoch ----
        network.train()
        total_loss = 0.0
        for xb, yb in loader:
            xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss = loss_function(network(xb), yb)
            loss.backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(network.parameters(), 5.0)      # keeps training stable
            optimizer.step()
            total_loss += loss.item() * len(xb)

        # ---- check the validation set ----
        val_probs = NeuralTextClassifier(network, settings["max_len"]).predict_proba(val_text)
        val_f1 = f1_score(y_val, val_probs.argmax(axis=1), average="macro", labels=ALL_CLASSES, zero_division=0)
        history.append((epoch, total_loss / len(y_train), val_f1))
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d} | train loss {total_loss / len(y_train):.4f} | val macro-F1 {val_f1:.4f}")

        # ---- early stopping ----
        if val_f1 > best_f1 + 1e-4:
            best_f1, epochs_without_gain = val_f1, 0
            best_weights = {k: v.detach().clone() for k, v in network.state_dict().items()}
        else:
            epochs_without_gain += 1
            if epochs_without_gain >= settings["patience"]:
                print("Stopping early (no improvement).")
                break

    network.load_state_dict(best_weights)             # go back to the best epoch

    # Learning curve
    h = pd.DataFrame(history, columns=["epoch", "train_loss", "val_macro_f1"])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3))
    ax[0].plot(h["epoch"], h["train_loss"]); ax[0].set_title("Training loss (should go down)")
    ax[1].plot(h["epoch"], h["val_macro_f1"]); ax[1].set_title("Validation macro-F1 (higher is better)")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    return network

Experiment 3: CNN¶

Idea: a 1D convolutional network slides small windows (3, 4 and 5 words wide) over the article. Each window detector learns to spot a key phrase (for example the name of a league or a minister). The strongest match of each detector is kept and used to classify. It is fast and works well for topic classification. Class weights are switched on so the rarer topics are not ignored.

In [19]:
class TextCNN(nn.Module):
    """Words -> embeddings -> window detectors -> strongest match -> classifier."""
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, emb_dim, kernel_sizes, n_filters, dropout, n_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, emb_dim, padding_idx=PAD)     # word number -> vector
        self.convs = nn.ModuleList([nn.Conv1d(emb_dim, n_filters, k, padding=k // 2) for k in kernel_sizes])
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)                                       # randomly switches off units (less overfitting)
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(n_filters * len(kernel_sizes), n_classes)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.embedding(x).transpose(1, 2)                                    # (batch, emb_dim, length)
        features = [F.relu(conv(x)).max(dim=2).values for conv in self.convs]    # strongest match per detector
        return self.classifier(self.dropout(torch.cat(features, dim=1)))

settings = {"max_len": MAX_LEN, "emb_dim": 100, "kernel_sizes": (3, 4, 5), "n_filters": 100, "dropout": 0.5,
            "class_weights": True, "lr": 1e-3, "batch_size": 64, "epochs": 6, "patience": 4}

def run_experiment(name, notes):
    """Train the CNN with `settings` and score it on the validation set.
    cv_scores is None: cross-validating a neural network 5 times is too slow."""
    network = TextCNN(len(vocab), settings["emb_dim"], settings["kernel_sizes"], settings["n_filters"],
                      settings["dropout"], N_CLASSES)
    network = train_network(network, settings)

    model = NeuralTextClassifier(network, settings["max_len"])
    val_probs = model.predict_proba(val_text)
    val_scores = get_scores(y_val, val_probs)
    cv_scores = None

    log_experiment(name, notes, settings, val_scores, cv_scores)
    return model, val_probs, val_scores, cv_scores

Experiment 4: BiLSTM with attention¶

Idea: an LSTM reads the article word by word and remembers the context. Bidirectional means it reads forwards and backwards. Attention lets the model learn which words matter most for the topic and focus on them, instead of treating all words the same.

In [21]:
class BiLSTMAttention(nn.Module):
    """Words -> embeddings -> BiLSTM -> attention (weighted average) -> classifier."""
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, emb_dim, hidden, dropout, n_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, emb_dim, padding_idx=PAD)
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(emb_dim, hidden, batch_first=True, bidirectional=True)
        self.attention = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * hidden, 2 * hidden), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(2 * hidden, 1, bias=False))
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(2 * hidden, n_classes)

    def forward(self, x):
        is_word = (x != PAD)                                              # True for real words, False for padding
        lengths = is_word.sum(dim=1).clamp(min=1)
        embedded = self.dropout(self.embedding(x))

        # "Pack" the articles so the LSTM ignores the padding
        packed = nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence(embedded, lengths.cpu(), batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False)
        output, _ = self.lstm(packed)
        output, _ = nn.utils.rnn.pad_packed_sequence(output, batch_first=True, total_length=x.size(1))

        # Attention: one score per word -> softmax gives weights that add up to 1
        scores = self.attention(output).squeeze(-1).masked_fill(~is_word, -1e9)
        weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=1)
        summary = (weights.unsqueeze(-1) * output).sum(dim=1)             # weighted average of the words
        return self.classifier(self.dropout(summary))

Experiment 5: BiLSTM with Word2Vec embeddings¶

Idea: so far the networks started with random word vectors. Word2Vec (skip-gram) first learns the vectors from our own training articles: words used in similar contexts get similar vectors. We then start the same BiLSTM + attention network from these vectors instead of random ones. (We train Word2Vec on the training articles only, so nothing leaks from validation or test.)

If this beats Experiment 4, good word embeddings help. If not, the network already learns enough by itself.

In [23]:
from gensim.models import Word2Vec

# 1) Train Word2Vec on the TRAINING articles only
w2v = Word2Vec(sentences=[tokenize(text) for text in train_text], vector_size=100, window=5,
               min_count=2, sg=1, epochs=10, workers=1, seed=SEED)          # sg=1 -> skip-gram
print("Word2Vec has learned vectors for", len(w2v.wv), "words")

# 2) Build the embedding matrix: row i = vector of the word with number i in our vocabulary
def make_word2vec_matrix(dim=100):
    matrix = np.random.RandomState(SEED).normal(0, 0.1, (len(vocab), dim)).astype("float32")   # random start
    matrix[PAD] = 0.0
    found = 0
    for word, number in vocab.items():
        if word in w2v.wv:
            matrix[number] = w2v.wv[word]                 # use the Word2Vec vector when we have one
            found += 1
    print(f"{found:,} of {len(vocab):,} vocabulary words have a Word2Vec vector")
    return torch.tensor(matrix)

settings = {"max_len": MAX_LEN, "emb_dim": 100, "hidden": 64, "dropout": 0.4,
            "class_weights": True, "lr": 1e-3, "batch_size": 64, "epochs": 6, "patience": 4}

def run_experiment(name, notes):
    """Train the BiLSTM (starting from Word2Vec vectors) and score it on the validation set."""
    network = BiLSTMAttention(len(vocab), settings["emb_dim"], settings["hidden"], settings["dropout"], N_CLASSES)
    network.embedding.weight.data.copy_(make_word2vec_matrix(settings["emb_dim"]))     # start from Word2Vec
    network = train_network(network, settings)

    model = NeuralTextClassifier(network, settings["max_len"])
    val_probs = model.predict_proba(val_text)
    val_scores = get_scores(y_val, val_probs)
    cv_scores = None

    log_experiment(name, notes, settings, val_scores, cv_scores)
    return model, val_probs, val_scores, cv_scores

Experiment 6: Transformer (AfroXLMR, fine-tuned)¶

Idea: a Transformer is a large network that was already pretrained on huge amounts of text. AfroXLMR was pretrained on 17 African languages, including Kinyarwanda and Kirundi. We only fine-tune it on our articles. This is usually the strongest approach for African languages because the model already "knows" the language.

It needs a GPU (for example a free Colab GPU). Without one, this cell is skipped automatically (the other experiments still run). Change TRANSFORMER_CHECKPOINT in the settings to try another model.

In [25]:
class TransformerTextClassifier:
    """Wraps a fine-tuned transformer so it has .predict_proba(texts) like every other model."""
    def __init__(self, network, tokenizer, max_len):
        self.network, self.tokenizer, self.max_len = network, tokenizer, max_len

    @torch.no_grad()
    def predict_proba(self, texts):
        self.network.eval()
        out = []
        for i in range(0, len(texts), 32):
            batch = self.tokenizer(list(texts[i:i + 32]), truncation=True, max_length=self.max_len,
                                   padding=True, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
            out.append(F.softmax(self.network(**batch).logits, dim=1).cpu().numpy())
        return np.vstack(out)

settings = {"checkpoint": TRANSFORMER_CHECKPOINT, "max_len": TRANSFORMER_MAX_LEN, "batch_size": 16, "lr": 2e-5,
            "epochs": 3, "class_weights": True}

def run_experiment(name, notes):
    """Fine-tune the transformer with `settings` and score it on the validation set."""
    from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer
    set_seed(SEED)
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(settings["checkpoint"])
    network = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(settings["checkpoint"], num_labels=N_CLASSES).to(device)

    # Turn all training articles into token ids once
    enc = tokenizer(train_text, truncation=True, max_length=settings["max_len"], padding="max_length", return_tensors="pt")
    loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(enc["input_ids"], enc["attention_mask"], torch.tensor(y_train)),
                        batch_size=settings["batch_size"], shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED))

    weights = None
    if settings["class_weights"]:
        w = compute_class_weight("balanced", classes=np.arange(N_CLASSES), y=y_train)
        weights = torch.tensor(w, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
    loss_function = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=weights)
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(network.parameters(), lr=settings["lr"], weight_decay=0.01)

    best_f1, best_weights = -1.0, None
    for epoch in range(1, settings["epochs"] + 1):
        network.train()
        total_loss = 0.0
        for ids, mask, labels in loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            logits = network(input_ids=ids.to(device), attention_mask=mask.to(device)).logits
            loss = loss_function(logits, labels.to(device))
            loss.backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(network.parameters(), 1.0)
            optimizer.step()
            total_loss += loss.item() * len(labels)

        model = TransformerTextClassifier(network, tokenizer, settings["max_len"])
        val_f1 = f1_score(y_val, model.predict_proba(val_text).argmax(axis=1), average="macro", labels=ALL_CLASSES, zero_division=0)
        print(f"epoch {epoch} | train loss {total_loss / len(y_train):.4f} | val macro-F1 {val_f1:.4f}")
        if val_f1 > best_f1:                                         # keep the best epoch
            best_f1 = val_f1
            best_weights = {k: v.detach().cpu().clone() for k, v in network.state_dict().items()}

    network.load_state_dict(best_weights)
    model = TransformerTextClassifier(network, tokenizer, settings["max_len"])
    val_probs = model.predict_proba(val_text)
    val_scores = get_scores(y_val, val_probs)
    cv_scores = None

    log_experiment(name, notes, settings, val_scores, cv_scores)
    return model, val_probs, val_scores, cv_scores

run_transformer = torch.cuda.is_available() if RUN_TRANSFORMER == "auto" else bool(RUN_TRANSFORMER)
if run_transformer:
    transformer_model, tr_val_probs, tr_val_scores, tr_cv_scores = run_experiment("transformer_afroxlmr", "Fine-tuned AfroXLMR with class weights.")
    register_model("transformer", "transformer_afroxlmr", transformer_model, tr_val_scores, tr_cv_scores, settings)
    print("Validation:", {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in tr_val_scores.items()})
    show_report("Transformer (validation)", y_val, tr_val_probs)
else:
    print("⏭️ Transformer skipped: no GPU found. Run this notebook on a Colab GPU (or set RUN_TRANSFORMER = True) to include it.")

Bonus experiment 7: Ensemble¶

Idea: different models make different mistakes. If we average their probabilities, many mistakes cancel out. No new training is needed.

In [26]:
class AverageEnsemble:
    """Averages the probabilities of several models."""
    def __init__(self, models):
        self.models = models
    def predict_proba(self, texts):
        return np.mean([m.predict_proba(texts) for m in self.models], axis=0)

members = [key for key in MODELS if key != "majority_baseline"]          # every real model (not the baseline)
print("Ensemble of:", members)
ensemble_name = f"ensemble_of_{len(members)}"

ensemble_model = AverageEnsemble([MODELS[key] for key in members])
ensemble_val_probs = ensemble_model.predict_proba(val_text)
ensemble_val_scores = get_scores(y_val, ensemble_val_probs)
log_experiment(ensemble_name, "Average of the probabilities of all models above.", {}, ensemble_val_scores, None)
register_model("ensemble", ensemble_name, ensemble_model, ensemble_val_scores, None, {"members": members})
print("Validation:", {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in ensemble_val_scores.items()})

9. Error analysis¶

A score alone does not tell us why a model fails. Here we study the articles that the chosen model classified wrongly on the test set:

  1. Which topics get mixed up?
  2. Which topics are hardest, and does that follow how many training articles they have?
  3. Do long articles fail more often?
  4. Was the model confident when it was wrong?
  5. What do the wrongly classified articles look like? (printed only if SHOW_ERROR_EXAMPLES = True)

All wrongly classified articles are also saved to a CSV file so you can read them and describe the reasons in your report.

How to explain the errors in your report¶

Use the tables above and the examples to discuss possible reasons. Typical reasons for news topic classifiers:

  • Overlapping topics. A news story about a minister opening a hospital is politics, health and economy at once. Check the confusion table: are most mistakes between related topics?
  • Rare topics. Topics with few training articles (look at the "training articles" column) give the model little to learn from. Compare the error rate with the number of training articles.
  • Long articles. The neural networks only read the first MAX_LEN words. If long articles fail more, the missing text may be the reason.
  • Noisy labels. We found articles whose identical text carried two different topic labels in the original data, so some "mistakes" may be questionable labels.
  • Source style. Articles come from different websites and newspapers with different writing styles.
  • Vocabulary. Kinyarwanda and Kirundi words have many prefixes and endings, so a word form never seen in training becomes <unk>. Models with sub-word input (the Transformer) handle this better.
  • Cleaning and duplicates. We removed duplicates so scores are honest, but this also reduced the data, especially for the small topics.

Tie each reason to evidence (a number from the tables or an example). That is what makes an error analysis convincing.

10. Deploy: save the model into the models/ folder¶

The web app must give exactly the same predictions as this notebook. So the next cells:

  1. save the chosen model into models/<dataset>/ (if the best model is the ensemble, all its members are saved),
  2. write api/nlp_utils.py from the same functions and classes used in this notebook (cleaning, tokenizer, networks), so the web app cannot drift away from the notebook,
  3. write api/requirements.txt with the library versions used here,
  4. test that the API's model gives the same probabilities as the notebook on 100 test articles.

Run this notebook once with DATASET = "kinnews" and once with DATASET = "kirnews": the web page then lets the user choose between both languages.

After it runs, start the FastAPI server from the project folder. It loads the models from models/ and also serves the HTML page:

pip install -r api/requirements.txt
uvicorn main:app --app-dir api --port 8000

then open http://localhost:8000 in your browser.

MODEL_DIR.mkdir(parents=True)

# 1) Which models does the API need? The best model on validation (an ensemble = all its members)
if best_model_name == "ensemble":
    deploy_keys = [k for k in MODELS if k not in ("ensemble", "majority_baseline")]
else:
    deploy_keys = [best_model_name]

# 2) Save each model in its own folder
config_models = []
for key in deploy_keys:
    model, folder = MODELS[key], MODEL_DIR / key
    folder.mkdir()
    settings_used = RESULT_INFO[key]["settings"]
    if isinstance(model, NeuralTextClassifier):
        torch.save(model.network.state_dict(), folder / "weights.pt")
        kind = "cnn" if isinstance(model.network, TextCNN) else "bilstm"
    elif isinstance(model, TransformerTextClassifier):
        model.network.save_pretrained(folder); model.tokenizer.save_pretrained(folder)
        kind = "transformer"
    else:                                          # scikit-learn pipeline (TF-IDF + classifier)
        import joblib
        joblib.dump(model, folder / "model.joblib")
        kind = "sklearn"
    config_models.append({"name": key, "type": kind, "path": key, "settings": settings_used})

if any(m["type"] in ("cnn", "bilstm") for m in config_models):
    (MODEL_DIR / "vocab.json").write_text(json.dumps(vocab, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")

# 3) Write api/nlp_utils.py: the SAME functions/classes as in this notebook + a small loader
def get_notebook_source(name):
    # Find the notebook cell that defined the function/class `name` and return exactly that code.
    # (Plain inspect.getsource does not work for classes defined in notebook cells.)
    for cell in reversed(get_ipython().user_ns["In"]):          # every cell that has been run
        try:
            tree = ast.parse(cell)
        except SyntaxError:                                     # skip cells with magics such as %pip
            continue
        for node in tree.body:
            if isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.ClassDef)) and node.name == name:
                return ast.get_source_segment(cell, node)
    raise ValueError(f"Could not find the code of {name}. Run the cells that define it first.")

PAD, UNK = 0, 1

"""

FOOTER = """
def encode_text(text, vocab, max_len):
    # One cleaned text -> tensor of word numbers, exactly max_len long (same as in the notebook)
    ids = [vocab.get(word, UNK) for word in tokenize(text)[:max_len]]
    return torch.tensor([ids + [PAD] * (max_len - len(ids))], dtype=torch.long)


class DeployedClassifier:
    # Loads the saved model(s) of ONE language and predicts the topic of ONE text.
    def __init__(self, model_dir):
        self.model_dir = Path(model_dir)
        self.config = json.loads((self.model_dir / "config.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        self.labels = self.config["labels"]
        vocab_file = self.model_dir / "vocab.json"
        self.vocab = json.loads(vocab_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) if vocab_file.exists() else None
        self.models = [self._load(entry) for entry in self.config["models"]]

    def _load(self, entry):
        folder, kind, s = self.model_dir / entry["path"], entry["type"], entry["settings"]
        n_classes = len(self.labels)
        if kind == "sklearn":
            import joblib
            return kind, joblib.load(folder / "model.joblib"), s
        if kind in ("cnn", "bilstm"):
            if kind == "cnn":
                net = TextCNN(len(self.vocab), s["emb_dim"], tuple(s["kernel_sizes"]), s["n_filters"], s["dropout"], n_classes)
            else:
                net = BiLSTMAttention(len(self.vocab), s["emb_dim"], s["hidden"], s["dropout"], n_classes)
            net.load_state_dict(torch.load(folder / "weights.pt", map_location="cpu"))
            return kind, net.eval(), s
        if kind == "transformer":
            from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer
            tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(folder)
            return kind, (tokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(folder).eval()), s
        raise ValueError("Unknown model type: " + kind)

    @torch.no_grad()
    def _probabilities(self, model, text):
        kind, obj, s = model
        if kind == "sklearn":
            return obj.predict_proba([text])[0]
        if kind in ("cnn", "bilstm"):
            return F.softmax(obj(encode_text(text, self.vocab, s["max_len"])), dim=1)[0].numpy()
        tokenizer, network = obj
        batch = tokenizer([text], truncation=True, max_length=s["max_len"], return_tensors="pt")
        return F.softmax(network(**batch).logits, dim=1)[0].numpy()

    def predict(self, raw_text):
        # Returns None for empty text, otherwise a dictionary with the topic, confidence and all probabilities.
        cleaned = basic_cleaning(raw_text)
        if cleaned == "":
            return None
        probs = np.mean([self._probabilities(m, cleaned) for m in self.models], axis=0)
        best = int(probs.argmax())
        ranking = sorted(zip(self.labels, probs), key=lambda pair: -pair[1])
        return {"label": self.labels[best], "confidence": float(probs[best]),
                "probabilities": {label: float(p) for label, p in ranking},
                "cleaned_text": cleaned}
"""

shared_code = "\n\n".join(get_notebook_source(name) for name in ("basic_cleaning", "tokenize", "TextCNN", "BiLSTMAttention"))
(API_DIR / "nlp_utils.py").write_text(HEADER + shared_code + "\n" + FOOTER, encoding="utf-8")

# 5) TEST: does the API's model give the same probabilities as this notebook?
import importlib
if str(API_DIR) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(API_DIR))
import nlp_utils
importlib.reload(nlp_utils)

api_classifier = nlp_utils.DeployedClassifier(MODEL_DIR)
n_check = min(100, len(test_text))
api_probs = np.array([[api_classifier.predict(text)["probabilities"][label] for label in LABELS] for text in test_text[:n_check]])
largest_difference = np.abs(api_probs - test_probs[best_model_name][:n_check]).max()
same_label = (api_probs.argmax(axis=1) == test_probs[best_model_name][:n_check].argmax(axis=1)).mean()

print(f"Largest difference between API and notebook probabilities: {largest_difference:.6f}")
print(f"Same predicted topic on {same_label:.0%} of the {n_check} test articles")
if largest_difference < 1e-3 and same_label == 1.0:
    print("✅ The API model matches the notebook.")
else:
    print("⚠️ The API differs from the notebook. Do NOT deploy yet. Check Section 10.")

11. All results in one place¶

This cell prints everything (data, every experiment, test scores, per-topic reports) and saves the same text to results/<dataset>/all_results.txt, ready to copy into your report.

In [36]:
report_lines = []
def say(text=""):
    print(text)
    report_lines.append(str(text))

def section(title):
    say("\n" + "=" * 72); say(title); say("=" * 72)

# 1. The data
section(f"1. DATA ({info['language']}, dataset = {DATASET})")
say(f"Split mode: {SPLIT_MODE} | topics ({N_CLASSES}): {LABELS}")
say(f"Original articles: {n_start:,} | removed empty: {n_empty:,} | conflicting labels: {n_conflict:,} | "
    f"duplicates: {n_dup_removed:,} | left: {n_start - n_empty - n_conflict - n_dup_removed:,}")
say(f"Topics removed for having fewer than {MIN_ARTICLES_PER_CLASS} articles: {too_small.to_dict() if len(too_small) else 'none'}")
say()
say(split_summary.to_string())

# 2. Every experiment that was run
section("2. ALL EXPERIMENTS (validation set, best first)")
say(log_table.drop(columns=["settings"]).round(4).to_string())
say()
for row in experiment_log:
    say(f"- {row['experiment']}: {row['notes']}")
    say(f"    settings: {row['settings']}")

# 3. Validation scores and cross-validation scores of each model
section("3. VALIDATION AND CROSS-VALIDATION SCORES")
for key, info_ in RESULT_INFO.items():
    v, cv = info_["val_scores"], info_["cv_scores"]
    say(f"{key:20s} validation: macro-F1 {v['macro_f1']:.4f} | weighted-F1 {v['weighted_f1']:.4f} | "
        f"accuracy {v['accuracy']:.4f} | log loss {v['log_loss']:.4f}")
    say(f"{'':20s} 5-fold CV macro-F1: " + (f"{cv['macro_f1_mean']:.4f} ± {cv['macro_f1_std']:.4f}" if cv else "not run"))

# 4. Test scores
section("4. TEST SCORES (the test set was used only once)")
say(test_table.sort_values("macro_f1", ascending=False).round(4).to_string())
say()
say(f"Chosen on validation: {best_model_name}")

# 5. Per-topic report of every model on the test set
section("5. PER-TOPIC REPORT ON THE TEST SET (every model)")
for name, probs in test_probs.items():
    say(f"\n--- {name}")
    say(classification_report(y_test, probs.argmax(axis=1), labels=ALL_CLASSES, target_names=LABELS,
                              zero_division=0, digits=3))

# 6. F1 per topic
section("6. TEST F1 PER TOPIC")
say(per_class.round(3).to_string())

RESULTS_DIR = ROOT / "results" / DATASET
RESULTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
(RESULTS_DIR / "all_results.txt").write_text("\n".join(report_lines), encoding="utf-8")
log_table.to_csv(RESULTS_DIR / "experiment_log.csv", index=False)
test_table.to_csv(RESULTS_DIR / "test_scores.csv")
per_class.to_csv(RESULTS_DIR / "test_f1_per_topic.csv")
say(f"\nAll of the above was also saved in: {RESULTS_DIR}")

How to read the results¶

  • Use macro-F1, not accuracy. Politics, sport and economy are big topics. A model can have high accuracy and still fail on the small topics.
  • Compare every model with the baseline. If a model is not clearly better than Experiment 0, it has learned nothing useful.
  • Look at each topic. One overall number can hide weak topics (see the per-topic table).
  • Small test topics are noisy. A topic with only a few test articles can swing several points. Say this in the report.
  • To improve a model: change the numbers in its settings dictionary, re-run that one experiment and compare the validation macro-F1 in Section 7.
